key_big: An acid donates H⁺; a base accepts H⁺.
body_html:
How to think about it

Brønsted–Lowry: an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Each acid has a conjugate base. Strong acids ionize completely; weak acids ionize only partly and have an equilibrium constant Ka.

pH = −log[H₃O⁺], pOH = −log[OH⁻], and pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴). A buffer resists changes in pH. In a titration, the equivalence point is reached when moles of acid equal moles of base.

Example

What is the pH of 0.010 mol/L HCl?

Strong acid: [H₃O⁺] = 0.010

Answer: 2.00

Example

What is the conjugate base of HCO₃⁻?

Remove one H⁺.

Answer: CO₃²⁻

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a weak acid is the same as a dilute acid.
  • Forgetting that pH is a log scale.
  • Writing the conjugate base with an extra H⁺.
